deep.reconstruction: This page has no mathematics. It is a fair-copy prose notebook entry in German Kurrent script, continuing a narrative of ancient Greek history (the Persian Wars) from the previous page. It reads like lecture notes or excerpts from a history course or textbook. Contents in order: (1) The Persian fleet under Datis and Artaphernes lands in Attica. The Athenians were unprepared ('Kriege' is corrected to 'Siege' above the line in a different ink). Instead of one commander they had elected 10 generals. (2) Miltiades is introduced as the 'saviour of Athens'. He came from a family that had earlier held power 'in Abydus', where he had learned Persian warfare and its weaknesses. (3) Each of the 10 generals held command for one day. The others voluntarily ceded their days to Miltiades, but he gave battle only on his own day of command. (4) The Persians were camped at Marathon. Miltiades had no more than 10,000 men and little cavalry, but made up for the shortfall with skill. He chose favourable ground and had trees felled where the Persian cavalry was to attack. The Athenians broke through and defeated the Persian army. (5) The Persians re-embarked to strike Athens directly, but Miltiades got there first and foiled the plan. (6) The Persians returned to Asia. The writer attributes this probably to a lack of provisions rather than to the defeat at Marathon. (7) The Spartans took no part in the victory because a national festival intervened. The next page completes the sentence and dates the battle 'c. 490, 29 Sept.' No derivation, computation or mathematical notation occurs. There is nothing to reconstruct mathematically.
errors: Historical slip in the source or the note-taker: Miltiades' family (the Philaids) held the tyranny of the Thracian Chersonese, not Abydos. Abydos lies on the Asian shore of the Hellespont opposite the Chersonese, and was ruled by a pro-Persian tyrant.

The figures (Persians: 100,000 infantry and 10,000 cavalry on the previous page; Athenians: 10,000) and the felling of trees against cavalry come from Cornelius Nepos (Miltiades 4-5). They are not reliable by modern standards. The 10,000 figure also omits the roughly 1,000 Plataeans.
The claim that the Persians withdrew mainly for lack of provisions is the lecturer's or writer's speculation. It is not attested in Herodotus.
Next page: the date '29 Sept.' reflects one older traditional reckoning. Modern estimates usually give August or September 490 BC (often 12 Sept., after Boeckh).
